name: Frank Miles
bio: George Francis ('Frank') Miles, portraitist of Society beauties - the editors note he 'did many drawings' of Lillie Langtry - awarded the Royal Academy's Turner silver medal on 10 December 1879 for a painting of an Ocean Coast. He shared rooms with Wilde at Thames House, 13 Salisbury Street, off the Strand, until August 1880, and then at Keats House, 1 Tite Street, Chelsea; the friendship dates from Wilde's Oxford years, with visits together at Bingham and Moytura in the mid-1870s per the General Index.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial notes, Complete Letters (2000), p. 78 n. 3, p. 86 n. 2, p. 91 n. 2, p. 94 n. 1; General Index entry, p. 1256
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 19 n. 1 (dates)
bio_note: DATES (added 2026-08-03): born 1852, died 1891, from the editors' first-mention footnote, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 19 n. 1 (repo PDF 44) - 'George Francis Miles (1852-91), son of the rector, was a popular artist in the early Eighties: his many drawings of Lillie Langtry did much to enhance her popularity. After he had shared two sets of rooms with Wilde in London they quarrelled and separated. Miles spent the last four years of his life in an asylum.' Located in the OCR mirror, then read as a rendered page image and the printed folio 19 confirmed. Years only in the source; no month or day recorded. The same footnote is the source for the asylum years, which the bio does not yet carry. All facts from editorial notes read as page images 2026-08-03: p. 78 n. 3 (Salisbury Street cohabitation to Aug 1880; repo PDF 103), p. 86 n. 2 (Turner medal; PDF 111), p. 91 n. 2 (Langtry drawings; PDF 116), p. 94 n. 1 (Keats House move; PDF 119), General Index p. 1256 (PDF 1301; 'W stays with, 17, 19, 20', Moytura 30-31). NO LETTERS SURVIVE. Established 2026-08-06 from the volume's Index of Recipients: Frank Miles HAS NO ENTRY. The only Miles listed is Alfred H. Miles (printed 542), a different man. Everything on this node therefore rests on mentions inside letters to other people, which is worth stating plainly given how much secondary literature is built on this relationship - and given that the Croft-Cooke claim tested and rejected on [[ward]] and [[harding]] was itself about mentions, not letters.
